statements: Theorem 1.1. The Parisi formula. The limiting expected log partition function per spin equals the infimum of the finite-level Parisi functionals.
Theorem 2.1. Guerra’s derivative formula. Guerra’s identity gives φ'(t) as a deterministic correction and a replica remainder, with an error controlled by c(N) under (1.3).
Equation (2.15). Guerra’s upper bound. Integrate the derivative bound from zero to one and insert the decoupled value at zero. The result is a finite-size upper bound for every admissible scheme.
Theorem 2.2. Convergence below time one. Choose t_0<1 first. A fixed-level minimizer sufficiently close to the unrestricted infimum gives convergence to the affine comparison at each t∈[0,t_0].

Theorem 2.4. Quadratic bound on constrained pressure. The constrained pressure lies below 2ψ(t) by a quadratic penalty in the distance from the target overlap, with an additive covariance error of 2c(N).
Proposition 2.5. Exponential bound on overlap probability. A fixed positive deficit below 2φ(t) in the constrained pressure makes the event of a prescribed overlap exponentially unlikely in N.
Differentiating in the Gaussian variance gives the heat term and the mass times the square of the spatial derivative.
Insert a level and vary its mass starting at the preceding mass. Near optimality prevents the first variation from being strongly negative.
At a minimizing breakpoint, the first variation in its location gives a stationarity identity. The equality relates a squared derivative of the recursion to the breakpoint itself.
Near the minimizing breakpoint, a Taylor estimate gives a lower bound on the curvature of the inserted-mass variation.
Proposition 5.7. Strict gap beyond neighboring breakpoints. Outside the two neighboring breakpoints, the interleaved recursion gives a strict pressure gap below 2ψ(t).

Interchanging two adjacent Gaussian operators increases their composition when the larger mass goes on the inside. For the strictly convex functions obtained from the Parisi recursion, positive variances and distinct masses give a strict inequality.
